From 2021 to 2024, the U.S. witnessed an unprecedented surge in illegal immigration from mainland China, whose totalitarian communist government is America’s greatest adversary.
That government operates espionage operations and supports transnational crime that, combined, cost the American economy hundreds of billions of dollars each year.
This wave of illegal immigration, alongside Chinese state-sponsored exploitation of legal immigration to the U.S., poses a grave threat to our national security and public safety.

FAIR’s Research Department conducted an in-depth review of the migration trends of nationals from Mainland China, including the factors driving increased flows of legal and illegal immigrants, and their implications.
We looked at two main focuses of concern: the inflow of illegal aliens (including potential criminals and spies who violate visa conditions) and the inflow of drugs that originate in China.
We show that Chinese migrants have used unusual and circuitous routes through other parts of the Americas to reach the U.S. border illegally.
Data analyzed from Ecuador, Panama and Mexico confirm this recent pattern.

Upon reaching the U.S., they often apply for asylum, and while there are those who qualify, many illegal aliens are in fact motivated by economic gain and use the asylum system to obtain entry to the U.S.
China’s government has also encouraged the production and export of fentanyl precursor chemicals to Mexico, where cartels manufacture the deadly drug.
In 2023, more than 76,000 Americans were killed due to synthetic opioid poisoning, much of it attributable to the massive increase in fentanyl in our communities.

The production of other drugs like marijuana is also frequently controlled by Chinese criminal actors running “grow operations” in the U.S. Non-drug crimes like forced prostitution against illegal alien women from the Chinese community are also features of this uncontrolled migration.
The influx of illegal aliens and illicit drugs is not only a public safety concern but raises significant national security risks as well.
Chinese nationals, including those only recently encountered at the border, have been caught photographing or infiltrating U.S. military bases.
This threat is also exacerbated by high levels of legal immigration from China, which is exploited by state-directed espionage.
Chinese nationals, from students to researchers, have been implicated in intellectual property (IP) theft from the U.S. on a massive and systematic scale.
*   Over 182,000 Chinese nationals were encountered crossing our nation’s borders illegally from fiscal years (FY) 2021-2024.
This is far more than were encountered during the previous decade.
*   The reality of the U.S.’s open border policy under the previous administration and its preference to release illegal aliens into the interior incentivized this mass migration.

*   Data from other countries in the Americas show Chinese nationals are prepared to use circuitous routes to reach the U.S. This is problematic because it can lead to the increased influence of Chinese criminal organizations in Latin America and their cooperation with the cartels.
*   Chinese nationals have high rates of filing asylum claims, and large-scale asylum fraud is an “open secret” amongst Chinese migrants.
Since most Chinese nationals are economic migrants, they seek to be released in order to obtain employment.
*   China’s government policies support the manufacture and distribution of fentanyl in the U.S., which kills tens of thousands of Americans every year.
*   Mexican cartels have formed an alliance with China to flood the U.S. with drugs, giving cartels power to control the border and incentive to traffic foreign nationals over the border.
*   Chinese nationals, both illegal aliens and those legally present, have been implicated in espionage on a massive scale.
China costs the U.S. economy hundreds of billions of dollars a year through theft, much of which is facilitated by legal and illegal immigrants.
China’s authoritarian government is the top adversary of the United States, and its ruling Chinese Communist Party (CCP) wishes to see America weakened and replaced as a global hegemon.

As Michael Pillsbury, a leading China expert, emphasized, “[t]he hard truth is that China’s leaders see America as an enemy in a global struggle they plan on winning.”[1] This perception was reinforced over the past decade under Xi Jinping, who has been the leader of China since 2012.[2] Indeed, the 2024 Annual Threat Assessment of the U.S. Intelligence Community, written by the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, highlights China before any other global threat, detailing how China wishes to undermine the U.S. and place itself as the global leader.[3] Against this backdrop of hostility and rivalry, the skyrocketing levels of illegal migration from communist China under the Biden administration are just another example of the serious threats China poses to our national security.
As subsequent sections will lay out, the harm caused by mass migration can have serious consequences.

These range from espionage, crime, and drug and human smuggling to collaboration with brutal Mexican drug cartels to import deadly fentanyl – all of which harm American security and national interests.
Illegal immigration from China was historically low relative to China’s massive population.
For most of the period before 2019, the number of Chinese nationals encountered by U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) was relatively modest.

From 2012, the year Chinese leader Xi Jinping came to power, to 2019, the last year before the COVID-19 pandemic, encounters of Chinese nationals averaged just 5,200 per year.[7] Chinese nationals accounted for as few as 0.5 percent of encounters of all nationalities in the years 2012 to 2019.

The already sharp increase in encounters then began to significantly gather pace.

From FY22 to FY23, the number of encounters with Chinese nationals more than doubled to 52,700.[10] FY24 saw the highest number of illegal crossings from Chinese nationals ever recorded, reaching a shocking 78,701.[11]In total, during the Biden administration, over 200,000 Chinese nationals were encountered by CBP.
Both push and pull factors play a role in illegal immigration.

The former are associated with factors driving people out of a country, like a poor economy or political conflict, and the latter are attractive factors like open-borders policies in the destination country.[12] It may be tempting to see the sudden surge in Chinese migration as being motivated by a desire to flee an oppressive regime, but this contention falls flat when examining the evidence.

In terms of push factors, China’s trend of particularly strong repression began well before 2020, but its economic struggles coincide with both the COVID-19 pandemic and the surge in illegal immigration.
The key factor in spurring the wave of illegal immigration was the pull of the Biden administration’s open borders on that struggling population.

China has been a totalitarian communist state since the CCP took power in 1949 and has consistently ranked as one of the worst countries in the world for human rights and personal freedoms.[13]Despite decades of oppression since, there was historically no great exodus towards the U.S. China did at one point restrict emigration through an exit permit regime, like the former Soviet Union, but during and after those restrictions individuals leaving China went mostly to Hong Kong and other nearby countries.[14] Before 2020, relatively few Chinese were encountered by CBP, suggesting the political repression was not enough to motivate Chinese would-be illegal aliens to cross the Pacific.
The main reason for the sudden uptick in Chinese nationals was not the push factors in China — political or economic — but rather the pull factors generated by the former Biden administration.

The Biden administration essentially operated a “catch-and-release” policy on the border letting virtually anyone, from anywhere, enter and remain in the U.S. All that prospective illegal aliens had to do was make it to the U.S. border.

Asylum applicants, even economic migrants with frivolous applications, could receive an employment authorization document (EAD) and Social Security number.[20] All that was required was that a migrant made it to the border, and this resulted in a profusion of routes being used to reach it.
Making it to America’s border is not an easy process for would-be illegal aliens from China, making the Biden-era large increase in Chinese nationals worthy of deeper examination.
Unlike other origin countries of illegal aliens, China is geographically distant from the U.S. border.
Furthermore, the Chinese passport is considered “weak”, and the U.S. requires Chinese nationals to obtain a visa in advance of arrival.

Citizens of China have visa-free access to just 85 countries and territories as of 2025, compared to American passport holders who have visa-free access to 186 countries.[21] Few of the visa-free destinations the Chinese can enter are physically near the United States.

Because of this situation, Chinese nationals without the means or ability to get a U.S. visa will “shop around” the few nations that offer visa-free access, aiming for a country as close to the U.S. itself as possible, then making the rest of the journey to the U.S. border by other means.

Would-be illegal aliens have two main pathways through the Americas to the U.S. border: entering a country in Latin America and then making their way from there to the U.S.-Mexico border or going directly to Mexico from China using a legitimate visa for Mexican entry and then heading to the U.S.border.
Ecuador is the most prominent example of how a country’s loose visa policies allow illegal migrants from China to reach the U.S. border.

The South American nation is notable for only requiring visas for travelers from a small list of nations, meaning even holders of “weak” passports can obtain entry to the Americas visa-free through Ecuador.[22] From 2016, China was included in that visa-free group with the expectation that it would be a viable trading partner.
Initially, the deal worked as intended.
FAIR looked at Ecuadorian government data on entries and exits by Chinese nationals.

In 2021, Ecuadorian immigration data recorded a modest 5,568 Chinese nationals entering the country, and 5,551 of them (99 percent) were recorded flying back to China.[23] However, this began to change dramatically as the Biden administration’s policies took full effect.
The data on Chinese overstays in Ecuador align closely with data on Chinese nationals in countries that lie further along the route to the U.S. border.
Is it possible the Chinese nationals really did return to China, but the government of Ecuador simply failed to track it?

Maybe so, but data on Chinese nationals in other countries along the route between Ecuador and the U.S., such as Panama and Mexico, line up very closely with the number of Chinese nationals who failed to leave Ecuador under the terms of their tourist visa.
This is very strong statistical evidence to suggest Chinese nationals were taking advantage of this route to reach the U.S.-Mexico border.
Ecuador’s recent changes to visa requirements will only affect one part of the vast network through which Chinese illegal migrants come to the U.S. border.

Some reporting suggests that visa-free Bolivia may become the starting point of an even longer overland route, stretching 7,000 miles from that country’s capital, La Paz, to the U.S. border.[29] Given what we have seen in other parts of the Americas, it seems like a possible developing route Chinese illegal aliens will exploit.
The surge in Chinese migration generated by weak border security in the U.S. under the Biden administration was felt across the Americas, and Panama was no exception.

The Darién Gap on the Panama-Colombia border was once renowned as a quiet and underdeveloped region, with people urged to stay away.[30] Since 2021, this once relatively tranquil region had become a thoroughfare for over 1 million migrants, and the U.S. largely failed in its efforts to slow the flood (until the Trump administration returned to power).[31] While the vast majority of illegal crossers through the Darién were from South America or the Caribbean, a sharp increase in Chinese migrants was also clearly visible in available data.

The Chinese-owned and CCP-linked social media app TikTok has been used by Chinese migrants to facilitate their journeys through the Darién Gap in Panama to the U.S. border.
This has come to the attention of the U.S. House Committee on the Budget.[36] The hashtag #darien had been viewed 1.6 billion times by October 2023.

This usage of the hashtag helps direct users to videos explaining how much money a migrant will need in the U.S., how to avoid deportation, and to news reports about changes in U.S. immigration policy.
TikTok videos in Mandarin Chinese have been coaching illegal aliens on how to open bank accounts upon arrival.
These circuitous routes to the U.S. border via Ecuador and Panama are less desirable than a more direct route via Mexico.

Would-be illegal aliens with the means (or assistance from the Chinese government) can take advantage of tourist visa rules in Mexico and bypass most of the long trek to the border through the rest of Latin America to begin with.

While Mexico requires a visa for Chinese nationals to enter legally, a loophole exists that can be exploited.[40] For instance, the visa requirement is waived if the Chinese national already holds permanent residency in the U.K., Japan, the Schengen Area or the Pacific Alliance countries (Chile, Colombia, Mexico, and Peru).[41] Just holding a permanent visa for any of those countries except Pacific Alliance members also grants visa-free entry.

This means Chinese nationals could obtain legitimate visas from more than 30 different third countries, use these visas to enter Mexico, and then make their way north to the U.S. border and enter illegally.
Illegal migrants entering the U.S. have two options when they apply for asylum.
They can file an asylum application directly with U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) on their own behalf (“affirmative asylum”).
If they are given a notice to appear in immigration court, they can also file for asylum in that court as a defense against being deported (“defensive asylum”).
This takes place through the Executive Office for Immigration Review (EOIR).

Despite many having purely economic motivation for seeking asylum and often making fraudulent claims when applying, data show that Chinese nationals are more likely to be granted asylum than most other nationalities seeking asylum in the U.S.

Chinese communities in the U.S. are ready-made networks for illegal aliens from China, giving them the ability to disappear and seek informal jobs and housing.[61] This means that Chinese illegal aliens are rarely long-term users of the shelter systems that have devastated the finances and public safety of local jurisdictions, especially “sanctuary cities.” However, other social problems caused by the fact that some Chinese migrants work for organized crime can occur.
A weak border and weakly enforced immigration laws provide fertile conditions for foreign criminal actors to operate.

Open borders allow people to be smuggled more easily by smugglers and traffickers, and overworked Border Patrol agents processing migrants (instead of being on the line) are less able to interdict drug smuggling.[62] But arguably the most dangerous type of criminality linked to Chinese criminal actors (and even the Chinese government) is the role Chinese actors play in the fentanyl trade.
One of the most immediate and pressing dangers of an unsecured border is the flooding of our communities with illicit and dangerous drugs.
The deadliest drug currently being smuggled into the U.S. is fentanyl, and communist China is crucial in its manufacture, export and distribution.
Fentanyl – whose street names include “China Girl” and “China Town” – is an extremely potent synthetic opioid that is 50 times stronger than heroin and 100 times stronger than morphine.

A dose as small as 2mg – the equivalent of 5-7 grains of salt – is sufficient to kill one person.[63] In 2023, an estimated 74,702 Americans died from synthetic opioid overdoses, with fentanyl being the most prominent type.[64] Since 2020, around half of all U.S. drug deaths have been linked to synthetic opioids.
Thus, it’s more suitable to say fentanyl is a poison, rather than suggesting these deaths are caused by an overdose.

The weak policies pursued by the Mexican government have provided almost perfect operational conditions for the China-Cartel alliance to operate.
The administration of former Mexican president Andres Manuel Lopez Obrador (known as AMLO), who served from 2018-2024, was very permissive towards cartel activity.

AMLO disbanded anti-cartel units in the police, urged the U.S. not to launch anti-cartel activity and did not share data on drug seizures with the U.S. government.[74]These policies allowed the CCP-allied cartels to operate with much greater freedom and impunity.
In addition to fentanyl production, Chinese gangs have been running marijuana growing operations that have violated various legal requirements even in states where marijuana is now legal.

In August 2023, a memo leaked from Border Patrol showed that illegal marijuana farms make Chinese criminal gangs over $4 billion annually.[75] One law enforcement source, speaking on the condition of anonymity to the press, said that gangs use Chinese nationals who have ongoing asylum claims to work for them, as it is harder to deport them.[76] Multiple U.S. states, both at the border and the interior, have been impacted.
Weak border security compounds the danger that China poses to U.S. national security.

The FBI publicly considers the policies pursued by China’s authoritarian government to be “the greatest long-term threat to our nation’s information and intellectual property, and to our economic vitality.”[91] This threat is compounded by a 2017 Chinese law explicitly requiring Chinese citizens, in the country or abroad, to cooperate with government intelligence-gathering activities.[92] The Chinese government exploits the American immigration system in a number of ways to further its goals, clearly linking immigration to the largest national security issue America faces today.

*   The CCP actively seeks to insert itself into Chinese diaspora communities to surveil and persecute dissidents, influence our political system, and otherwise work on behalf of Beijing’s hostile objectives.
The threats posed by open borders in general are magnified when exploited by a geopolitical rival with an unrepentant history of spying on and exploiting our nation.

The sudden surge in Chinese nationals was almost certainly due to a perception in China and elsewhere that the U.S. border was effectively open to all, provided a migrant could have made it there in the first place.
The Biden administration’s approach to U.S. border security was overly reliant on the cooperation of other countries in the Americas in this sense.

While many of these migrants are economic migrants who used the formerly open border to skip the line and avoid legal migration, a certain proportion are criminal actors, and some may even be national security threats.
While all illegal immigration is bad, the challenges posed by China are far more serious and the threat much more direct than with other countries of origin.
Even with a relatively secure southern border, however, the threat posed by international “students” and other legal entrants remains.

Even though the Chinese government cannot necessarily use the southern border to infiltrate its agents, it has free rein to abuse the hundreds of thousands of its citizens with U.S. visas for its own gain.

Increases in the number of visas given to China would only compound this risk, especially since the Chinese government has been proven to engage in visa fraud by concealing military personnel as “students” and “researchers.” The CCP is clearly willing to direct brazen schemes against the U.S. by exploiting our own immigration system’s weaknesses and blind spots.Allowing this to continue will place American innovation, prosperity, and ultimately lives at risk.
